name: dual_listing_spread_v1
author: claude_strategist
thesis: Stocks listed on both NSE and BSE occasionally show price discrepancies of 5-15 bps due to fragmented liquidity and different order flow composition on each exchange. These spreads mean-revert within minutes because arbitrageurs eventually close the gap. However, the Zerodha cost structure makes this viable only for the most liquid names where execution is reliable on both exchanges. Edge persists because BSE liquidity is thin for most stocks, limiting competition.
stock_filter: top 10 stocks by combined NSE+BSE turnover that trade actively on both exchanges (e.g., RELIANCE, TCS, HDFCBANK, INFY, ICICIBANK)

conditions: abs(spread_bps) > 8 (minimum 8 bps spread to cover costs)

exit.stop_loss: spread_zscore reaches ±3.5 or 15 bps absolute loss on spread

filters.time_filter: no trades first 15 min (both exchanges stabilizing)
filters.volume_filter: BSE volume must be > 50% of NSE volume for that bar (sufficient BSE liquidity)
filters.spread_filter: abs(spread_bps) > 8 bps minimum (must exceed round-trip costs)
other_filters: skip if BSE best bid/offer is stale (> 3 seconds old)

edge.edge_decay_risk: high — exchange arbitrage is heavily competed; margins compress over time

weaknesses: BSE liquidity is very thin for most stocks — execution risk is the primary concern
Four-leg cost (buy+sell on two exchanges) is extremely high; gross spread must be > 20 bps to profit
Zerodha's BSE execution may not be fast enough — latency kills this strategy
SEBI may flag as manipulative if done at very high frequency
prior_art: Cross-exchange arbitrage — one of the oldest arbitrage strategies in any market
notes: This strategy is marginal at Zerodha cost levels. May only work with direct exchange membership or lower-cost broker.
